project_name: Pinecrest Mill kraft lignin cake (fictional): dashboard assessment
disclaimers: Fictional demo data: the Pinecrest Mill and this lignin stream are invented. All values are illustrative assumptions, not measurements from any real mill, and must be replaced with a mill's own lab data before any decision.
BioValue AI gives indicative decision support. It does not guarantee profitability, does not verify customer demand, and does not constitute engineering approval.

Gross margin, profitability, NPV, and IRR are not calculated. They need capital costs, fixed costs, a discount rate, a time horizon, and agreed definitions, none of which are available yet. Gross contribution excludes capital costs, fixed costs, and the value of the feedstock in its current use.
Scores use a 1-5 scale. A criterion that was not assessed lowers data completeness; it is never counted as a low score.

constraints: The lignin is currently used as internal boiler fuel, so diverting it to sale would affect that fuel use.
There is no lignin dryer; buyers needing dry powder would require drying before use.
The stream leaves as wet cake, and uncertain moisture affects dry tonnage and shipping mass.
Molecular weight, phenolic hydroxyl content, and sodium content are missing, limiting pathway and ash-related specification checks.
There is no fractionation or chemical-modification equipment available on site.
data_quality_notes: The record is fictional demo data: all values are illustrative assumptions, not measurements from a real mill.
The lignin-content method is stated for illustration only and should be confirmed before comparing with buyer specifications.
Moisture is marked uncertain; the recorded annual quantity, moisture, composition, and dry-matter ranges are assumed rather than measured.
Validation passed the dry-matter balance, composition-total, and missing-figure/data-gap checks.
agent.summary: Validated fictional profile: 40,000.0 t/yr wet cake at 0.35000000000000003 moisture fraction gives 26,000.0 t/yr dry mass. Validation reported no inconsistencies; use only as a demonstration until replaced with mill measurements.

carbohydrates_pct.method: Total sugars after acid hydrolysis (stated for illustration)

data_gaps.impact: Every figure in this profile is invented for demonstration. Results based on it say nothing about a real mill.
data_gaps.next_step: Replace the profile with the mill's own lab data and production records.

data_gaps.impact: Molecular weight can't be compared with any pathway requirement until it is measured.
data_gaps.next_step: Commission a lab analysis of molecular weight distribution, and record the method used.

data_gaps.impact: Phenolic hydroxyl content can't be compared with any pathway requirement until it is measured.
data_gaps.next_step: Commission a lab analysis of hydroxyl group content, and record the method used.

data_gaps.impact: The make-up of the ash is unknown, so ash-related requirements can only be checked against total ash.
data_gaps.next_step: Request an inorganic element analysis of the ash.

data_gaps.impact: Reported lignin content depends on what the analysis counts. The method here is stated for illustration only.
data_gaps.next_step: Confirm the analytical method with the lab and use the same one when comparing with buyers' specifications.

data_gaps.impact: Moisture sets the dry tonnage (dry matter = wet quantity x (1 - moisture)) and the mass that has to be shipped.
data_gaps.next_step: Log cake moisture for each shift over at least one month.

checks.disclaimer: Fictional demo data: the Pinecrest Mill and this lignin stream are invented. All values are illustrative assumptions, not measurements from any real mill, and must be replaced with a mill's own lab data before any decision.

current_use.description: Fictional: the precipitated lignin is fired in the mill's own boilers in place of purchased fuel. The unit was built to relieve the recovery boiler, not to sell lignin.

geographic_market.logistics: Fictional: rail siding at the mill; the nearest deep-water port is assumed to be about 150 km away.

supported_claims.EV-PF-01#1: For kraft lignin in phenol-formaldehyde (PF) resins, the typical replacement of phenol is up to 50%, using a two-step process with depolymerized lignin (Mw 800-1,700 g/mol).
supported_claims.EV-PF-01#2: Kraft lignin needs an activation or depolymerization step before use in PF resins.
supported_claims.EV-PF-01#R1: Pre-treatment of kraft lignin: Activation or depolymerization is needed before kraft lignin is used in PF resins.
supported_claims.EV-PF-02#2: UPM states that LPF resin is industrially proven and meets EN 314-2 Bonding Class 3 for veneer plywood.
supported_claims.EV-PF-02#3: UPM reports formaldehyde emissions (EN 717-2) of 0.230 mg/m²/h for 12 mm spruce, 0.148 for 12 mm birch, and 0.170 for 12 mm combi panels made with LPF resin.
supported_claims.EV-PF-01#4: Global PF resin production was expected to reach about 10 Mt (valued at about USD 13.36 billion in 2019), and more than 50% of these resins are used to make adhesives for wood-based panels.
supported_claims.EV-PF-04#2: With the depolymerized lignin making up 50% of the phenolic component, the resin's viscosity, bonding strength, and free formaldehyde met the Chinese wood-adhesive standard used in the study.

applications.statement: Kraft lignin can partially replace phenol in phenol-formaldehyde resins used for plywood and other wood-based-panel adhesives, with activation or depolymerization needed in the reviewed kraft-lignin process.
Lignin-phenol-formaldehyde resin has been reported for veneer plywood, with a vendor reporting compliance with EN 314-2 Bonding Class 3 and formaldehyde-emission results under EN 717-2.

target_customers.statement: Plywood and other wood-based-panel manufacturers are the implied customers for lignin-based PF adhesive.

competing_materials.statement: Phenol in conventional phenol-formaldehyde resin is the material lignin replaces.

qualification_requirements.statement: The reviewed kraft-lignin PF route requires activation or depolymerization before use.

The vendor reports LPF resin meeting EN 314-2 Bonding Class 3 for veneer plywood and provides formaldehyde-emission results measured under EN 717-2; the evidence does not establish these as universal requirements for all lignin-based PF resins.
A laboratory study tested viscosity, bonding strength, and free formaldehyde against a Chinese wood-adhesive standard, but the paper names that standard inconsistently.

limitations: The reported replacement levels summarize published studies and are not results from a single commercial plant.
The vendor's performance and cost claims are manufacturer claims without a cited test report; its lignin is not identified as kraft lignin and its composition is not provided.
The TRL estimate is from a 2018 report and concerns biobased phenolic resins generally, not specifically kraft-lignin resin.
The laboratory study used poplar plywood samples and names its Chinese standard inconsistently.
missing_information: No lignin price, demand or sales volume, named resin or panel buyers, contract terms, or regional market demand is provided.

Evidence does not establish whether Pinecrest's wet cake meets process or product specifications; its molecular weight, phenolic hydroxyl content, sodium content, and moisture are missing (feedstock:missing_properties).

market_evidence.rationale: The evidence includes a vendor claim of industrially proven LPF resin and a plywood bonding-class result, alongside laboratory work, but does not document lignin-resin sales to established buyers.

supported_claims.EV-PU-01#1: Replacing 30 wt% of the petroleum-based polyol with unmodified lignin, 16 of the 19 lignins tested gave rigid PUR/PIR foams that passed all measured ASTM C1029-15 type 1 specifications.
supported_claims.EV-PU-01#2: Two of the three foams that failed were made with kraft lignin; they failed the compressive strength and/or closed-cell content requirements.
supported_claims.EV-PU-03#1: Fifteen unmodified lignins (ten kraft, five organosolv) were tested as a replacement for 20 wt% of the petroleum-based polyol in flexible polyurethane foam.
supported_claims.EV-PU-03#3: Organosolv lignins were the most suitable for automotive flexible foam; kraft lignins gave denser, stiffer foams that the authors suggest may suit heavy-duty foams.
supported_claims.EV-PU-04#2: In cited studies, kraft lignin replaced up to about 20% of polyol after oxypropylation, up to 50% when depolymerized and oxypropylated, and up to 100% when liquefied in a bio-based polyol.
supported_claims.EV-PU-04#R1: Modification of kraft lignin: Kraft lignin needs significant treatment (for example oxypropylation, depolymerization, or liquefaction) to reach target properties for polyurethanes.
supported_claims.EV-PU-01#R1: Total hydroxyl value of the lignin: Above 200 mg KOH/g (3.56 mmol/g total OH) is cited as the acceptable range for rigid polyurethane foam production. This is total OH, not phenolic OH, so it is not checked against the feedstock's phenolic OH figure.
supported_claims.EV-PU-04#3: Bio-based polyurethanes, including the small lignin-based share, hold less than 1% of the polyurethane market.

applications.statement: Lignin has been tested as a partial replacement for petroleum-based polyols in rigid PUR/PIR insulation foams; study results vary, including kraft-lignin samples that failed measured specifications.
Unmodified lignin has also been tested in flexible polyurethane foam, with the authors suggesting kraft-lignin foams may suit heavy-duty uses rather than automotive flexible foam.
Reviewed kraft-lignin polyurethane routes include oxypropylation, depolymerization, or liquefaction to reach target properties.

target_customers.statement: Rigid insulation-foam producers are an implied customer type for lignin-containing PUR/PIR foams.

Flexible-foam producers serving automotive or heavy-duty applications are implied customers; the study identifies automotive suitability for organosolv lignins and suggests heavy-duty uses for kraft-lignin foams.

competing_materials.statement: Petroleum-based polyols are the incumbent material partially replaced by lignin in the reviewed polyurethane studies.

qualification_requirements.statement: One study assessed rigid PUR/PIR foam against ASTM C1029-15 type 1 specifications; it reports that some kraft-lignin foams failed compressive-strength and/or closed-cell-content requirements.
The study cites total hydroxyl value above 200 mg KOH/g (3.56 mmol/g total OH) as acceptable for rigid polyurethane foam; this is total hydroxyl content, not phenolic hydroxyl content.
The review states that kraft lignin needs significant treatment, such as oxypropylation, depolymerization, or liquefaction, to reach polyurethane target properties.

limitations: Most performance evidence is from laboratory foams; one study tests mixed lignin types and does not provide a kraft-only pass rate.
A rigid-foam study was published in 2013, and organosolv lignin performed better than kraft lignin in that study.
Flexible-foam testing was laboratory scale and compared results with automotive OEM requirements; sulfur odor was noted but not measured.
The TRL estimate applies to a broad set of polyurethane uses rather than kraft-lignin foams specifically; replacement levels are each from single studies.
A review of commercialization challenges was available only as an abstract.
missing_information: No lignin price, product or feedstock volumes, named buyers, contracts, or regional demand is documented; the market-size figures in the evidence are dated and do not quantify demand for Pinecrest lignin.

The evidence does not establish Pinecrest's suitability against total-hydroxyl or foam-performance criteria; its phenolic hydroxyl content and other composition data are missing (feedstock:missing_properties).
There is no on-site fractionation or chemical-modification equipment, and buyers requiring dry powder would require drying before use (feedstock:constraints).

market_evidence.rationale: Evidence shows research-scale testing and review-level discussion of a small lignin-based share of the polyurethane market, but it does not document commercial lignin-foam trials, pilots, or sales.

supported_claims.EV-CM-01#1: Oak Ridge National Laboratory (ORNL) specifications for lignin as a carbon fiber precursor (Baker et al. 2005) set lignin content at 99%, ash below 0.1%, volatiles below 5% at 250 °C, and full removal of particulates larger than 1 µm.
supported_claims.EV-CM-01#2: A fifth precursor specification was later added: residual carbohydrates below 500 ppm (Baker 2011).
supported_claims.EV-CM-01#3: None of the lignin samples in the study met the ORNL volatiles specification.
supported_claims.EV-CM-04#2: Hard carbons from kraft lignin (carbonized at 1,200 °C) had higher initial coulombic efficiency than those from sulfonated lignin, which the review attributes to lower ash content.
supported_claims.EV-CM-05#1: Activated carbon has no strict limitations on precursor quality, so lignin too impure for other uses can be converted into it.
supported_claims.EV-CM-06#2: Stora Enso announced a EUR 10 million pilot production line for lignin-based anode material, operational in 2021, with scale-up planned in standardized 20 kton manufacturing units.
supported_claims.EV-CM-02#1: DOE's goal was to cut industrial-grade carbon fiber cost from about $20/lb to a target of $5-7/lb, with mechanical properties suitable for automotive use (250 ksi tensile strength, 25 Msi modulus).
supported_claims.EV-CM-06#1: Stora Enso states that qualification with battery manufacturers and carmakers can take 3 years, and that partnering helps shorten this.
supported_claims.EV-CM-03#2: The modelled production cost of GreenLight lignin-based carbon fiber was EUR 12.6/kg, against about EUR 16/kg estimated for PAN-based fiber; cooperation with existing melt-spinning and carbon fiber plants could lower it to EUR 6.5-7.1/kg.
supported_claims.EV-CM-04#1: A feedstock comparison for sodium-ion battery hard carbon lists lignin at about 300 $/t with a carbon yield above 40%, against anthracite (50-200 $/t, about 90%) and cellulose (1,000 $/t, below 10%).
supported_claims.EV-CM-01#R1: Lignin content: Greater than 99% (ORNL precursor specification).
supported_claims.EV-CM-01#R2: Ash content: Below 0.1% by weight (ORNL precursor specification).
supported_claims.EV-CM-01#R3: Residual carbohydrates: Below 500 ppm (Baker 2011). Not mapped to the feedstock's carbohydrate percentage, because the source doesn't state the basis of the ppm figure.
supported_claims.EV-CM-01#R4: Volatile material: Below 5% at 250 °C. The feedstock profile has no volatiles field, so this is not checked.
supported_claims.EV-CM-01#R5: Particulate matter: 100% removal of particulates larger than 1 µm in diameter.
supported_claims.EV-CM-02#R1: Purification of kraft lignin: The kraft lignin examined needed purification before it could be used for carbon fiber.
supported_claims.EV-CM-02#R2: Melt spinnability of softwood lignin: A plasticizing (alloying) agent is needed to melt-spin softwood lignin.
supported_claims.EV-CM-05#R1: Precursor quality: No strict limitations on precursor quality; lower ash improves yield.
supported_claims.EV-CM-05#3: Higher ash in the lignin lowered activated carbon yield and carbon conversion.
supported_claims.EV-CM-03#1: The GreenLight project raised the TRL of lignin precursor fiber production from 2-3 (proof of concept) to 5 (validated in an industrially relevant environment).

applications.statement: Lignin is studied as a precursor for carbon fiber, but this route has stringent precursor specifications and the cited study found none of its samples met the volatile-material specification.

Kraft lignin is studied as a precursor for hard carbon in sodium-ion battery applications; a review reports higher initial coulombic efficiency for hard carbon made from kraft lignin than from sulfonated lignin in the cited comparison.
Lignin can be used as a precursor for activated carbon, including in a laboratory study using zinc chloride activation.
Lignin-derived hard carbon has also been developed as lithium-ion battery anode material, with a company announcing a pilot production line.

target_customers.statement: Carbon-fiber precursor and carbon-fiber producers are implied customers for purified, processable lignin precursor.
Sodium-ion battery anode-material producers are implied customers for lignin-derived hard carbon.
Activated-carbon producers are implied customers for lignin used as a carbon precursor.
Lithium-ion battery manufacturers are implied customers for lignin-based anode material; the cited company also describes qualification with battery manufacturers and carmakers.

competing_materials.statement: PAN-based carbon fiber is identified as a competing fiber material.
Anthracite is identified as a competing hard-carbon feedstock.

qualification_requirements.statement: The cited ORNL carbon-fiber precursor specifications call for lignin content greater than 99%, ash below 0.1% by weight, residual carbohydrates below 500 ppm, volatile material below 5% at 250 °C, and removal of particulates larger than 1 µm.
The kraft lignin examined for carbon fiber required purification, and softwood lignin requires a plasticizing or alloying agent for melt-spinning according to the cited report.
A company states qualification with battery manufacturers and carmakers can take 3 years; the evidence gives no corresponding universal battery qualification standard.
The activated-carbon study reports no strict precursor-quality limitations, while noting that lower ash improves yield and carbon conversion.

limitations: The carbon-fiber precursor specifications are cited secondhand, apply to carbon fiber rather than hard or activated carbon, and the cited study used a non-standard-kraft lignin source.
The carbon-fiber report is from 2009 and reports lignin-based fiber mechanical properties at about 50% of its target; the GreenLight cost figures are modeled rather than measured.
Hard-carbon evidence is a review summarizing other studies; the activated-carbon evidence is laboratory-scale and uses zinc chloride activation.

The lithium-ion battery evidence is company investor material with forward-looking statements; it describes plans as of 2021, whose later status was not verified, and supplies no lignin quality specifications.
missing_information: No current prices, market volumes, named buyers, contracts, or regional demand are provided for Pinecrest lignin or the three carbon-material routes.

Pinecrest's ash/sodium and other relevant composition and processing properties are not established; its sodium content and molecular weight are missing, and the wet-cake moisture is uncertain (feedstock:missing_properties; feedstock:constraints).
The evidence does not provide a Pinecrest-specific process design, qualification result, or readiness assessment for any of the carbon-material applications.

market_evidence.rationale: The evidence includes a carbon-fiber development project validated in an industrially relevant environment and a company-announced anode-material pilot line, but it does not document established commercial sales by lignin producers.

processing_requirements.statement: The reviewed kraft-lignin PF route needs activation or depolymerization before use.
Pinecrest has no on-site fractionation or chemical-modification equipment, and drying would be needed if a buyer requires dry powder.
The reported vendor qualification results cover veneer plywood bonding and formaldehyde emissions, but they are not established as universal requirements for all lignin-based PF resins.

technical_maturity.statement: The cited LignoBoost-plus-resin route is reported at TRL 9; this is route-level evidence, not a Pinecrest-specific demonstration.

adoption_barriers.statement: Activation or depolymerization and the absence of on-site chemical-modification equipment make a partner or new processing assets necessary.
Pinecrest lignin's molecular weight, phenolic hydroxyl content, sodium content, and moisture are missing, so product and process fit remain unverified.
No named resin or panel buyers, contracts, regional demand, or lignin pricing are documented.
Diverting lignin from the existing boiler use could affect mill fuel supply.

missing_inputs: Named buyers, contract terms, regional demand, and a Pinecrest-specific product qualification result are also unavailable.
assumptions: Scenario analysis used fictional wet feedstock masses of 36,000.0 / 40,000.0 / 43,000.0 t/yr and moisture assumptions of 40.0 / 35.0 / 30.0%; availability assumptions were 40.0 / 50.0 / 60.0%.
The economics tool did not calculate product output, revenue, variable cost, gross contribution, or contribution per tonne because yield, price, and variable costs were missing.

uncertainties: The compatibility tool returned no score because the evidence library has no numeric requirements for this pathway.
Economics are indeterminate without yield, price, and variable costs; feedstock moisture and dry tonnage for shipping are uncertain.
The cited route-level readiness and reported vendor performance do not establish Pinecrest-specific qualification or commercial access.

commercialization_feasibility.rationale: A commercial route is identifiable, but activation or depolymerization, missing on-site modification equipment, and unresolved feedstock qualification mean significant investment or a partner is needed. Named buyers and project-specific economics are also absent.

feedstock_compatibility.rationale: The evidence library has no numeric requirements for this pathway to check against.

technical_readiness.rationale: TRL 9 maps to 5. Stated in EV-PF-03#1.

indicative_economics.rationale: Gross contribution per tonne could not be calculated. Missing inputs: product yield, product price, variable costs.

report.summary: The scoring engine ranks polyurethanes first and carbon materials second, while phenolic resins remain unranked for insufficient assessed data. Treat this as a validation priority, not an investment decision: polyurethane's lead depends heavily on assumed economics, carbon has a documented compatibility gap for its checked fiber route and no assessed economics, and resin's strong route-level maturity is offset by missing compatibility and economics evidence.

documented_facts.statement: For kraft lignin in phenol-formaldehyde (PF) resins, the typical replacement of phenol is up to 50%, using a two-step process with depolymerized lignin (Mw 800-1,700 g/mol).
Kraft lignin needs an activation or depolymerization step before use in PF resins.
Pre-treatment of kraft lignin: Activation or depolymerization is needed before kraft lignin is used in PF resins.
UPM states that LPF resin is industrially proven and meets EN 314-2 Bonding Class 3 for veneer plywood.
UPM reports formaldehyde emissions (EN 717-2) of 0.230 mg/m²/h for 12 mm spruce, 0.148 for 12 mm birch, and 0.170 for 12 mm combi panels made with LPF resin.
Global PF resin production was expected to reach about 10 Mt (valued at about USD 13.36 billion in 2019), and more than 50% of these resins are used to make adhesives for wood-based panels.
With the depolymerized lignin making up 50% of the phenolic component, the resin's viscosity, bonding strength, and free formaldehyde met the Chinese wood-adhesive standard used in the study.
Replacing 30 wt% of the petroleum-based polyol with unmodified lignin, 16 of the 19 lignins tested gave rigid PUR/PIR foams that passed all measured ASTM C1029-15 type 1 specifications.
Two of the three foams that failed were made with kraft lignin; they failed the compressive strength and/or closed-cell content requirements.
Fifteen unmodified lignins (ten kraft, five organosolv) were tested as a replacement for 20 wt% of the petroleum-based polyol in flexible polyurethane foam.
Organosolv lignins were the most suitable for automotive flexible foam; kraft lignins gave denser, stiffer foams that the authors suggest may suit heavy-duty foams.
In cited studies, kraft lignin replaced up to about 20% of polyol after oxypropylation, up to 50% when depolymerized and oxypropylated, and up to 100% when liquefied in a bio-based polyol.
Modification of kraft lignin: Kraft lignin needs significant treatment (for example oxypropylation, depolymerization, or liquefaction) to reach target properties for polyurethanes.

Total hydroxyl value of the lignin: Above 200 mg KOH/g (3.56 mmol/g total OH) is cited as the acceptable range for rigid polyurethane foam production. This is total OH, not phenolic OH, so it is not checked against the feedstock's phenolic OH figure.
Bio-based polyurethanes, including the small lignin-based share, hold less than 1% of the polyurethane market.

Oak Ridge National Laboratory (ORNL) specifications for lignin as a carbon fiber precursor (Baker et al. 2005) set lignin content at 99%, ash below 0.1%, volatiles below 5% at 250 °C, and full removal of particulates larger than 1 µm.
A fifth precursor specification was later added: residual carbohydrates below 500 ppm (Baker 2011).
None of the lignin samples in the study met the ORNL volatiles specification.
Hard carbons from kraft lignin (carbonized at 1,200 °C) had higher initial coulombic efficiency than those from sulfonated lignin, which the review attributes to lower ash content.
Activated carbon has no strict limitations on precursor quality, so lignin too impure for other uses can be converted into it.
Stora Enso announced a EUR 10 million pilot production line for lignin-based anode material, operational in 2021, with scale-up planned in standardized 20 kton manufacturing units.
DOE's goal was to cut industrial-grade carbon fiber cost from about $20/lb to a target of $5-7/lb, with mechanical properties suitable for automotive use (250 ksi tensile strength, 25 Msi modulus).
Stora Enso states that qualification with battery manufacturers and carmakers can take 3 years, and that partnering helps shorten this.

The modelled production cost of GreenLight lignin-based carbon fiber was EUR 12.6/kg, against about EUR 16/kg estimated for PAN-based fiber; cooperation with existing melt-spinning and carbon fiber plants could lower it to EUR 6.5-7.1/kg.
A feedstock comparison for sodium-ion battery hard carbon lists lignin at about 300 $/t with a carbon yield above 40%, against anthracite (50-200 $/t, about 90%) and cellulose (1,000 $/t, below 10%).
Lignin content: Greater than 99% (ORNL precursor specification).
Ash content: Below 0.1% by weight (ORNL precursor specification).
Residual carbohydrates: Below 500 ppm (Baker 2011). Not mapped to the feedstock's carbohydrate percentage, because the source doesn't state the basis of the ppm figure.
Volatile material: Below 5% at 250 °C. The feedstock profile has no volatiles field, so this is not checked.
Particulate matter: 100% removal of particulates larger than 1 µm in diameter.
Purification of kraft lignin: The kraft lignin examined needed purification before it could be used for carbon fiber.
Melt spinnability of softwood lignin: A plasticizing (alloying) agent is needed to melt-spin softwood lignin.
Precursor quality: No strict limitations on precursor quality; lower ash improves yield.
Higher ash in the lignin lowered activated carbon yield and carbon conversion.
The GreenLight project raised the TRL of lignin precursor fiber production from 2-3 (proof of concept) to 5 (validated in an industrially relevant environment).
A techno-economic comparison lists LignoBoost extraction combined with phenol substitution in resins ('LB+Resin') at TRL 9.
The IEA rates polyurethane uses of lignin (foams, panels, coatings, rubber replacement; kraft, organosolv, and soda lignin) at TRL 6.
